@Corwin: Happens more than you'd think. People hear "missing woman, brown hair, about this tall" and it's half the villages in the Realm.

Walking the same road a third time with him is stranger than you expected - he narrates it under his breath without seeming to notice he's doing it, _she'd have stopped here, she always stopped here, the water's good_, like the route itself has become a kind of prayer.

narrative:
Camp that night is quieter than the ones before it - not worse, just heavier, the way a search feels different once it has produced something, even something small. Corwin sits a little apart from the fire, turning the day's information over like a coin he doesn't yet trust to spend.

This is where the search actually is right now: not resolved, not abandoned, just genuinely, unglamorously still going.

narrative:
It's the innkeeper, in the end - or the guild clerk, or your own patience in the square, whichever road brought you here - who happens to mention that a woman answering to Essa runs a small bakery near the mill now, has for close to three years. Before you can go to her, Corwin stops you.

@Corwin: Before we do this. There's something you should probably know. Our parents had arranged a marriage for her, back home. To a man twice her age, for reasons that had everything to do with a debt and nothing to do with her. I knew. I didn't stop it. I told myself it wasn't my place, that our parents knew best, that she'd be provided for. She never forgave me for that, near as I can tell, since she left the same season the wedding would have happened - and never told me where.

narrative:
You bring Corwin in without warning either of them properly, and it goes exactly as raggedly as an unprepared reunion after three years and a hidden marriage tends to go - too many words at once, some of them unkind, all of them honest. It's not the clean reconciliation you might have hoped for. It's real, though, messy and loud and entirely theirs.

By the time it settles, something between them has at least been said out loud that wasn't for three years. Whether that's enough is a question that belongs to the two of them now, not to you.

narrative:
@Corwin: I keep going back and forth. She's clearly built something real here. Showing up might undo that, just by existing near it. Not showing up means I found her and said nothing, which feels like its own kind of betrayal, just a quieter one.

He looks at you like the decision genuinely isn't only his to make anymore - which, three winters and a river crossing later, it probably isn't.

narrative:
Corwin writes a short letter instead of walking in - no demands in it, no explanation of the years, just enough to say I know where you are now, and I'm not going to make that your problem. He leaves it with the net-mender back in the fishing village to pass along eventually, rather than deliver it himself.

@Corwin: If she wants to answer, she knows where the road usually finds me. If she doesn't, I think - I think I can actually live with that now. Which is new.

narrative:
You watch Corwin fold the map away for what feels like the first time in three years without immediately smoothing it back out to look again. He doesn't go to the bakery. He doesn't write a letter. He just turns, finally, back toward the road, carrying the not-knowing instead of fighting it.

@Corwin: Three years, I think, is exactly as long as I needed to spend looking. However that sounds. I found out what I actually needed to know - that she's alive, and safe, and happier without my help than she'd have been with it. That's not nothing. I used to think it was nothing. It isn't.
